prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: These, FrenchKisses, Why

outputs.L1:
I give thanks to the spiders’ webs and the circus dancers who stain our eyes with rapid movements and authorize our handcuffs to make no distinction between night and day, or love and hate.

No one will know the sum of our arduous daily separations from bed to work. These pillars, in truth, belong to you, since I have not counted them, nor do I know any more than you where they are, or in what country they still exist.

We can place all our concerns into a loaf of bread and French kisses, go to the movies, and watch the splashing milk on the screen imitate the forest in the moonlight. Why all the fuss about the patrons becoming feathers, discharging their ideas of nobility on the evening news? There are no lights in the theater—only soft snow from the balcony, which is the little red schoolhouse where all this began.

Actually, it was because of you that I did not attend as often as I should have. I was too embarrassed to face you across the clay-modeling tables, since I always felt that the clay in your hands was a cartoon version of my teen years, dear slippery-fish ladies of the sleepy West.

Don’t forget: my early life will be yours, too, with its self-descriptions of poetic justice. The tiny creatures we write about can describe themselves in the moss we leave behind.
outputs.L2:
I offer my gratitude to the cobwebs and to the acrobats of the circus, those who mark our vision with swift motion and permit our restraints to ignore any difference between darkness and daylight, affection and hatred.

No one will ever calculate the full total of our difficult everyday departures, from bed toward labor. These columns are really yours, because I have never numbered them, nor do I know any better than you where they stand, or in which nation they may still remain.

We are able to tuck every worry we have into a piece of bread and into French kisses, then go to the cinema and look at the milk splattering across the screen, pretending to be a forest under moonlight.

Why make such a commotion over the audience turning into feathers, spilling their notions of grandeur onto the nightly news? The theater has no illumination—only gentle snow falling from the balcony, which is also the small red schoolhouse where everything started.

In truth, it was on account of you that I failed to appear as regularly as I ought to have. I felt too ashamed to sit opposite you at the clay-sculpting tables, because the clay between your fingers always seemed to me like a caricature of my adolescent years, beloved slick-fish women of the drowsy West.

Remember this: my beginnings will belong to you as well, along with their accounts of poetic justice. The miniature beings we put into words are capable of telling their own stories in the moss we abandon after us.
outputs.L3:
The speaker reflects on the small separations that shape everyday life. Ordinary routines are presented alongside emotional opposites: night and day, love and hate, closeness and distance. These contrasts suggest that life is made up of repeated departures and returns, and that even familiar patterns can carry deep feeling.

At the same time, the poem imagines that shared worries and private anxieties can be softened or transformed. What begins as concern becomes something ordinary and comforting: bread, kisses, and movies. These simple pleasures show how human connection can make difficulty more bearable. Rather than treating emotion as abstract or dramatic, the poem brings it into the world of daily gestures and physical experiences.

The theater becomes an especially important space in the poem. It is not only a place to watch films but also a dreamlike setting where different parts of life overlap. Memory, childhood, and imagination blend together there, creating a space where the past can return in unexpected ways. The theater allows the speaker to move between reality and fantasy, suggesting that art can preserve feelings and memories that might otherwise be lost.

The speaker also admits to avoiding someone, not out of indifference, but because of embarrassment and vulnerability. This avoidance is connected to youth, a time when emotions often feel intense, exposed, and difficult to express. The confession reveals the speaker’s insecurity and suggests that personal relationships are shaped as much by fear and hesitation as by affection.

By the end, the poem connects intimate experience with larger ideas of history and justice. Personal memory becomes part of a broader poetic order, where even small details matter. The traces left behind by tiny living things suggest that nothing disappears completely. Lives, feelings, and actions leave marks, however faint, and the poem finds meaning in these delicate remains.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores intimacy, memory, daily labor, and artistic self-consciousness through a series of surreal and associative images. Its world is built from webs, theaters, classrooms, clay, bread, and kisses—ordinary and symbolic materials that continually shift in meaning. A web may suggest connection, entanglement, fragility, or the delicate structure of memory itself. A theater evokes performance and self-awareness, implying that identity is partly staged, revised, and observed. A classroom introduces learning, repetition, and the shaping of the self through experience, while clay and bread connect the poem to the physical labor of making: molding, kneading, feeding, and transforming raw matter into something meaningful. The image of the kiss brings these broader concerns back to the body, to affection, desire, and the intimate exchanges through which people remember and are remembered.

Through these images, the poem suggests that personal history is never entirely private. Memory passes through touch, language, work, and imagination, becoming shared with others and altered in the process. The speaker seems aware that art does not simply record experience; it reshapes it, giving form to what might otherwise remain fleeting or silent. Everyday gestures and materials become charged with significance, as if the smallest remnants of a life—a mark, a taste, a lesson, a touch—can carry emotional and historical weight. In this way, the poem presents art as a means of transformation. It allows the personal to become communal, the ordinary to become strange, and the transient to endure. Even the smallest traces of life are shown to have the power to speak beyond the self.
outputs.L5:
**These FrenchKisses: Why They Feel So Meaningful**

These moments we remember most are often the simplest ones: a glance, a smile, a quiet pause, or a kiss that says more than words ever could. **FrenchKisses** have long been seen as a symbol of passion, closeness, and emotional connection. They are not just about romance; they can represent trust, affection, and the desire to be fully present with another person.

**Why** do they feel so powerful? Because a kiss can communicate feelings that are difficult to explain. It can turn an ordinary moment into something unforgettable. Whether shared at the beginning of a relationship or after years together, FrenchKisses remind us of the beauty of intimacy and the importance of genuine connection.

In the end, these small expressions of love often become the memories we hold onto the longest.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem in the style of John Ashbery, with strange enjambments, dreamlike imagery, and reflections on childhood, work, theater, and memory.
counterfactuals.output:
At noon the office put on its antlers  
and everyone bowed to the copier, which was snowing.

I had been a child there once,  
under the conference table, listening to adults  
invent weather with their shoes.  
A pencil rolled toward me like a little train  
from a country where no one had to answer the phone.

Outside, the theater was rehearsing its windows.  
The actors wore clocks instead of faces,  
and the understudy for my mother  
kept forgetting the line about supper.  
How strange, to applaud a room  
for pretending to be another room.

Work, meanwhile, went on polishing its apple.  
The manager floated by in a gondola of memos,  
asking if the moon had submitted its hours.  
I said yes, though really it had been hiding  
in the break room, eating from a paper cup.

Memory is not a drawer but a stagehand  
moving furniture in the dark.  
You turn and the crib is a desk,  
the desk a coffin, the coffin a boat  
painted the exact blue of a Tuesday you lost.

Once I believed every street led home.  
Now home is the street, passing me slowly,  
with all its houses looking away.  
A red curtain rises in the lunch pail.  
Inside, my childhood stands on a chair  
reciting the alphabet to an empty field.

No one knows when the performance begins.  
We have been clapping for years.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental free-verse poem that sounds like a translated avant-garde text: dense, associative, slightly absurd, with images of spiders, circus dancers, bread, movies, snow, school, clay, and moss.
counterfactuals.output:
In the school of snow  
the blackboard exhales a spider.

No one translates the bell correctly.  
It arrives as bread,  
hard at the edge, warm in its political center,  
and the children put their ears to the crust  
to hear the old movies walking backward.

A circus dancer bends like a question  
trained by wolves,  
her ankles full of clay,  
her mouth a small theater  
where the tickets dissolve before the kiss.

I was there, or I was an umbrella.  
The sentence has lost its passport.  
Moss grows on the director’s chair,  
green applause for the film that never burns,  
though the projector is made of winter  
and the reel is a nest of nervous legs.

Spiders descend with scholarly patience.  
They annotate the ceiling.  
They say: history is not a horse  
but the dust beneath the horse  
remembering hooves.

Outside, bread falls softly from the sky.  
Inside, snow learns to sit upright at a desk.  
The teacher, wearing a mask of flour,  
asks us to sculpt our names from clay  
and then forget the alphabet.

The circus dancer turns once, twice,  
until the room becomes a round wound  
full of music and moss.  
Her skirt is a republic of torn posters,  
her shadow a silent movie  
where every face is waiting  
for weather to explain itself.

At recess the spiders play violins  
inside the loaves.  
The schoolyard glitters with teeth.  
Someone has buried a camera under the snow  
so the earth may dream in black and white.

I offer my hands to the mud.  
They return as small animals.

The lesson continues:  
bread is a window with hunger behind it,  
snow is a cinema for the blind,  
clay is the sleep of statues,  
moss is the soft error of stone.

And the circus dancer,  
still translating her body  
from fire into grammar,  
steps carefully over the spiders  
as if over signatures  
on a treaty between the impossible  
and the ordinary morning.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a long surrealist paragraph-poem about daily life, embarrassment, art class, and poetic justice, using unexpected metaphors and minimal punctuation.
counterfactuals.output: Each morning I button my shirt like a guilty museum closing its eyelids and the kettle shrieks as if it has remembered my childhood in a language made of steam I walk to work with toast crumbs in my pocket small blond witnesses to the crime of hunger and the buses kneel at the curb like tired elephants wearing advertisements for paradise everyone is carrying a face they borrowed from a drawer and mine is already wrinkled with apologies by the time I reach the art class where the plaster hands point nowhere and the fruit bowl poses with the arrogance of little planets I sit before my paper and try to draw a pear but it becomes my grandmother’s silence then a green fist then a moon ashamed of its own bruises the teacher says observe the negative space so I stare at all the things I have not said until they begin to sketch me back in charcoal and bad timing someone laughs when my chair makes a trumpet of my humiliation and suddenly my ears are two red lamps in a hotel for insects my stomach folds itself into an envelope addressed to nobody while the whole room pretends not to be a courtroom of smirking statues even the erasers look smug with their soft white alibis I want to crawl under the table and become gum stuck to the underside of history but the linoleum blooms into a river and carries my embarrassment past the easels past the sink clogged with watercolor sunsets past the cabinet where the scissors sleep open mouthed like silver fish waiting for ankles then poetic justice arrives not as thunder or a judge but as a pigeon wearing my teacher’s glasses and carrying a tiny diploma in its beak it lands on the model stand and knocks over the perfect arrangement of apples and bottles and dried flowers so the still life becomes suddenly honest rolling bruised and clattering across the floor like escaped thoughts everyone bends to gather the fruit and their own forgotten awkwardness spills from their sleeves one student blushes blue another sneezes glitter another confesses he has been drawing the same shoe for six years because it resembles his father’s disappointment and the laughter changes shape from knives into bread we pass it counterfactuals.prompt: Create a stream-of-consciousness poem addressed to an unnamed “you,” blending romance, labor, cinema, childhood school memories, and bizarre images like handcuffs, feathers, milk, and tiny creatures.
counterfactuals.output:
You come in like the projector coughs awake,  
a white square trembling on the wall of the break room,  
and I am still wearing my work gloves, still smelling of metal,  
sugar, oil, the long blue fatigue of Tuesday,  
but there you are, flickering,  
all wrist-bone and weather,  
all almost.

I wanted to tell you during recess, years ago,  
when the bell was a silver animal in the ceiling  
and chalk dust made ghosts of our hands,  
that your name felt like milk left out in moonlight,  
but I had a lunchbox, a loose tooth,  
a fear of multiplication,  
so I swallowed it  
and grew around the silence.

Now the factory doors open and close like eyelids.  
Now the boss counts minutes like beads.  
Now the conveyor belt brings me one more little moon,  
one more screw, one more dented tin star,  
and I think of your mouth saying nothing in the dark cinema  
while cowboys died beautifully  
and rain streaked the window outside  
as if the whole city were being developed in chemicals.

You, you, you—  
not a name, a match struck under water.  
I carry you in my apron pocket with the bent nails,  
the receipt, the feather I found stuck to a handcuff,  
don’t ask, the world is always leaving clues  
too strange for the police,  
too tender for the saints.

At night tiny creatures come out from behind the radiator,  
thumb-sized horses, glass ants, a moth wearing spectacles,  
and they ask if I have finished loving you yet.  
I tell them labor is never finished.  
I tell them the heart punches in, punches out,  
steals a smoke behind the loading dock,  
goes home with sore knees  
and dreams in Technicolor.

Remember school? No, of course you don’t,  
or maybe you remember differently:  
the map of the world peeling at the corners,  
the teacher’s red pen like a small wound,  
the smell of paste, wet wool, cafeteria milk,  
how we lined up two by two as if entering an ark  
and I tried to stand behind you  
just to study the weather of your hair.

There was a film once where lovers ran through wheat  
with no money and no plan,  
only the horizon unraveling gold thread,  
but my love, my almost, my unnamed you,  
we have time cards, bus transfers, cracked heels,  
we have rent due and onions to chop,  
we have feathers stuck in the sink drain  
and handcuffs hanging from the doorknob  
like a joke the angels forgot to explain.

Still, when you turn toward me—  
even in memory, even in the grainy cinema of the skull—  
the machines hush.  
The milk rises in its glass.  
The tiny creatures kneel in their tiny cathedral.  
My childhood desk opens and spills its crayons,  
its erasers, its secret notes never passed.

I want to write you on the steamed-up window.  
I want to clock in beside you forever.  
I want to be the scene where the audience leans forward,  
not knowing if anyone will kiss,  
not knowing if the train will arrive,  
not knowing why the sky is full of feathers  
and every feather is falling upward.

You are not here,  
which is one kind of presence.  
You are here,  
which is another kind of work.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an imitation of mid-century American surrealist poetry with disjointed syntax, odd capitalization, intimate confession, and dream logic.
counterfactuals.output:
At 3 A.M. the refrigerator began  
to call me Mother.

I was alone, except for the blue chair  
wearing my father’s hat  
and the moon, that old aspirin, dissolving  
in a glass of window.

Dear Nobody—  
I have kept your letters in my shoe.  
They have walked me into churches, bus stations,  
the soft red mouth of a Tuesday.  
Forgive me. I was born with a little staircase  
inside my chest  
and every night someone goes down it  
carrying a lamp.

The horses in the wallpaper  
are coughing again.  
One says my name as if it were a match  
struck underwater.  
One says Love is a pantry  
where the cans face inward.

O Small God of Linoleum,  
I have lied.  
I said I wanted a life  
but I meant a room with one orange in it,  
and a hand on my hair  
not asking anything.

In the dream, my brother is a snowman  
driving a black taxi through Kansas.  
He will not turn around.  
The meter is full of bees.  
I pay him with my teeth.

Morning comes in wearing gloves.  
It touches the spoons.  
It touches the mirror  
until my face returns, badly folded.

Listen—  
the city is kneeling in its overcoat.  
The pigeons have elected a queen.  
Her crown is made of bread and weather.

I open my mouth  
and a little white dog runs out,  
barking at the furniture of Heaven.

This is my confession:  
I loved the wrong door.  
I knocked until my knuckles bloomed.  
I entered and found only a bed,  
a bowl of rain,  
and my own body asleep there,  
murmuring,

Yes, Yes,  
I remember the fire  
before it became a house.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
